name: Daria Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and a junior agent on the contact-centre calls and chats. I finished secondary school and worked in a flower stall before I started here, so I can calm a disappointed customer but still need help on complicated refunds. I use the approved AI sorter every day to find the latest promise in a long chat, then check the original order. My pay is about usual for the job, although I am still below the experienced agents at handling exceptions.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Lio works part-time at a print shop, and our grown children live separately. We rent our flat and have five months of expenses saved. Some other centres are within reach by bus. I hope I can choose fewer hours later in life, but we have not settled what would pay for them; I like catching a wrong refund before the customer has to call again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the desk AI Plateau sounds like my sorter finding the latest order in a long chat. I would still check the customer’s original payment before approving a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the queue stays busy enough for me to learn the hard cases. Five months saved makes rent less frightening than it used to be, though Lio’s print-shop hours still move around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering order calls and using the sorter each day while checking the payment record. In the first year of small change, I’d transfer a fixed part of each pay packet into our rent reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the queue, watchful about a false refund. A quick summary cannot return money that was never sent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which refund did you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a summary said a refund was complete when the order only showed approval. I opened the payment tab with a senior agent before telling the customer anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep adding to savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lio (my husband) and I have five months saved already. I would add to it when my shifts stay regular rather than ask our grown children for money.

think: I think I can **learn harder cases** while the queue remains.
I know **variable print-shop hours** still affect our rent budget.

feel: **Calm** about calls, watchful about false refunds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may move simple order questions into software, but a customer still needs someone when a refund goes to the wrong card. I would ask for paid correction hours alongside any new speed figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose junior chat shifts, even though I like learning new systems. Lio’s part-time print wage and five months saved give us a search window, not a full replacement for my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new refund-routing tool by testing twenty old card corrections on a paid shift if a supervisor lets me log mistakes. In the first year simple chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid order-support role only if my hours fall and its written weekly wage and hours cover rent after bus fare; I’d keep paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, interested in what the tool actually misses. A faster answer can send a customer back to the wrong card twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the test count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the wrong-card returns and the minutes an agent spends fixing each one. I would show those numbers to the supervisor with the paid rota beside them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another centre worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the full week after bus fare, not just the hourly rate. Some nearby centres pay for too few shifts to cover our flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my sister and the desk that AGI by 2028 could settle a whole refund without asking a junior agent. I would ask the nearby garden centres for posted paid plant-care openings rather than wait for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my simple chats could vanish quickly in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later for hands-on work, and five months saved is useful but has a last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d apply for a posted paid plant-care job only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent after bus fare, and ask for a paid trial shift if offered. In the first year after 2028, I’d accept that work only after a signed offer still meets those terms; until then I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about calls, but I can begin a real search. Five months of savings gives me time to test soil and wages, not permission to work for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a plant trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to lift trays and water the outdoor plants for one paid shift. I remember the flower stall, but my back and the hours have to work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lio compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lio (my husband) and I would compare the bus journey and the actual full week before I sign. I would not spend our rent reserve on an unpaid trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives a few years to learn plant care if there is a paid place to use it. I would ask for posted nursery hours before taking a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn stock and plant health over five years, but robots around 2034 may later reach physical nursery work. I do not want a course badge that cannot pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded plant-care course on paid time only if a posted paid nursery opening requires it, and try a paid nursery shift if offered and lifting is safe. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer showing written weekly wage and hours covering rent after transport; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about switching, but I can inspect a real nursery before I leave the phones. A plant label is no substitute for a weekly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to learn which leaves show disease and how to lift a heavy tray without straining my back. A course should put me beside an experienced grower, not just a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lio check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Lio (my husband) the posted hours and bus fare before enrolling. A late nursery shift has to leave us both a workable journey home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 leaves time to compare paid work and keep learning on the calls we still have. I would ask for yearly junior paid-hour figures instead of a count of answered chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could earn and save for years if the queue remains, though thinking AI may still take calls in 2036. Five months saved is not a settled income for whatever comes after full-time work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking calls and transfer a fixed amount from each pay packet into our rent reserve. In the first year after 2036, if call hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid garden-centre role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent after transport; I would leave calls only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about 2036, secure enough about the next rota. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls gives me time to add to savings, not a guaranteed retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the full garden-centre week after bus fare with the call-centre wage. A new job is useful only if the whole week still pays rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have separate budgets. Lio (my husband) and I would not put their pay in our future plan without asking, and we do not intend to ask.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because daily use of a small sorter would not save the simple chats I am paid to answer. Five months saved gives us time to look, but rent still arrives every month. A posted paid plant-care role with written wages and hours covering rent after transport, a paid trial and any required employer-funded training on paid time would help; I would leave calls only after a signed offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the first person who spots a wrong refund can make someone fix it. My daughter has her own rent and cannot be the spare wage in our plan.

headlineQuote: My daughter has her own rent and cannot be the spare wage in our plan.
portrait: At **58**, Daria is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and flower-stall work.
She and Lio rent with **five months saved**, typical pay and some nearby call-job options.
She uses **AI daily** but still needs help with complex refunds.
She tests **plant-care work** before risking the household wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove simple chats despite her daily AI use.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid plant role**, rent-covering hours, paid trial and funded required training would help.
